evidence_quotes.quote: These findings were combined into a coding framework and used to design and analyse interviews with 19 key informants within national and local regulators.
The selected locations, Kenya, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia, are described in detail in the ESAWAS publication on sanitation regulatory journeys [55].
Even where manual handling is accepted by the national regulator, there may be local bylaws which effectively criminalise the practice.
At the most extreme, local regulators were working in a legal grey zone, enabling incremental improvements to manual handling and disposal but still effectively working outside the law.
All of the national and local regulators interviewed indicated that engaging informal manual emptiers, and enabling them to work safely, was an important part of reaching universal access.
The focus of formalisation was on improving practices, rather than the bureaucratic processes. Tacit amnesties until safe practices were feasible were frequently cited.

country.comment: Five positive-outlier case countries in East and Southern Africa selected for primary key informant interviews and legal/regulatory framework comparison (preliminary secondary data used to inform the interview guide drew from 5 UNICEF global regions).
country.where_found: PDF p. 5, Table 2; PDF p. 6, Section 2.5; PDF p. 7, Table 3

effect_estimate.comment: Primary qualitative study; no quantitative effect estimates are reported. Headline findings synthesize cross-country key informant interviews on regulatory practice and road-transported sanitation scaling.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across all five countries, utilities and municipalities operate as de-facto local regulators of road-transported faecal sludge emptying and transport alongside national regulators, despite implicit/unclear statutory mandates, severe resource constraints, and fragmented enforcement powers across health, environment, labour, and construction departments (including local bylaws that criminalise manual pit emptying even when permitted nationally). All interviewed national and local regulators identified proactively engaging and supporting informal (and often illegal) manual pit emptiers—via trust-building, safe consultation spaces, training, tacit amnesties, negotiated interim disposal sites, and incremental practice improvements rather than punitive sanctions or bureaucratic formalisation—as essential to extending safe sanitation access to low-income urban areas, requiring institutional and personal 'moral courage' to operate in legal grey zones.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 7–10, Sections 3.2–3.5.2; PDF pp. 11–13, Sections 4.1–4.3

mechanism_certainty.comment: Qualitative study appraised with CASP (design ceiling = 2). Directly documents regulatory and administrative mechanisms operating on urban road-transported sanitation provision through interviews with 19 senior national and local regulator officials and country legal/regulatory mapping.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 7, Table 3; PDF pp. 7–10, Sections 3.3–3.5.2

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines utility/authority service-area mandates and legal eligibility of manual emptying (service_area), de-emphasising bureaucratic licensing paperwork in favour of safe operating practices (procedural_steps), extra-legal regulatory discretion and local reinterpretation of rules (discretion), tacit amnesties and negotiated interim disposal sites (accommodation), training and capacity support for informal emptiers (bureaucratic_assistance), consultation spaces with informal emptiers (participation), overlapping/conflicting mandates and bylaws across national regulators, utilities/municipalities, and health/environment/labour/construction departments (institutional_fragmentation), inter-departmental coordination platforms and ministry/board advocacy (political_coordination), and fines/criminalisation vs deferral of penalties (sanction).
